citation: "Wolf's Point and the Town of Chicago." Chicagology. Transcribing the Chicago Magazine of 15 May 1857 — the account of the Wolf's Point settlement built on George Davis's 1832 drawing and on Gurdon S. Hubbard's own description of the place as he found it in 1818 — with A. T. Andreas and modern editorial matter around it.

transcribes.work: Chicago Magazine, 'Wolf's Point' — the account of the settlement at the forks, engraved from George Davis's 1832 drawing and incorporating Gurdon S. Hubbard's description of Chicago as he first saw it in 1818
transcribes.note: Carries the Miller House's log construction ('a log structure partly sided') and the Wolf Point Tavern's ('partly log and partly frame'), the fact of a frame element on each, and — through Hubbard — the marshy river-shore strip that grades the south division's marsh surface in terrain_spec.json. Twenty-five years after the fact, from a resident's drawing and a named witness speaking to the writer: rung 2.

note: Transcribes period and near-period accounts. Source for: the West Side as open prairie free from timber; the South Side timber belt running east to Wells and crossing Clark; the North Side 'thrifty heavy growth of timber'; the marshy river-shore strip of tall grass, reeds and rushes; the Public Square pond where Indians trapped muskrat and settlers hunted ducks; the slough draining that pond past the Tremont House site to the river at the foot of State Street; wild onions among the sedge grass. It is also where the two forks buildings are described in one sentence each: the Miller House 'was a log structure partly sided', Wentworth's tavern at the Point 'was partly log and partly frame'. RE-READ 2026-08-10, AND THE CITATION WAS WRONG. This record said the page compiles Andreas and the Fergus Historical Series. The body is the Chicago Magazine of 15 May 1857, whose author is writing twenty-five years after the scene it describes, from a resident's 1832 drawing and from Gurdon S. Hubbard's account given directly to him — 'This is a picture of Chicago, and of all that then composed it, as described to us by Gurdon S. Hubbard, Esq.' That is near-primary recollection, so the record moves from tier 4 to tier 2 on the document rather than on the host. Andreas is on the page too, carrying the town-limits chronology and the 1830 Thompson plat, and no claim here rests on it through this page — `andreas_1884_v1` is cited directly. The modern gallery captions and a CBS news item at the foot are later editorial matter and carry nothing. chicagology_prefire276 transcribes the SAME 1857 magazine and is still graded 4; nothing in the dataset cites it, so it is left rather than regraded unread. A LIMIT THAT MATTERS FOR MILLER'S HOUSE. What this page attests is 'partly sided' — that part of the building was frame-clad. It does NOT say two storeys and it does not say the range fronted the river; those are drloih_hotels' words, and `form.frame_addition_stories` accordingly still rests on that blog alone. A finding aid for images — re-source them from the holding institution before use. THE WOLF SIGN PASSAGE, READ 2026-08-21 FOR T-0072, AND WHERE IT SITS ON THE PAGE MATTERS. The page carries, in a NOTE at its foot rather than in the 1857 magazine body: “Wentworth was ambitious, and wanted a sign to attract wayfarers. Lieutenant Allen made one for him out of a piece of a box. He painted a picture of a wolf on it. The fort blacksmith made hinges, and the wolf sign was hung on a sapling. The tavern was the first institution to have a sign board in Chicago.” That is the only description this project holds of how the Wolf Point board was made, decorated and hung, and it is the reason the tavern's sign now flies from a pole rather than a wall bracket. ITS OWN AUTHORITY IS WEAKER THAN THIS RECORD'S TIER. The note names no author and cites nothing; it reads as the page compiler's summary of the standard retellings, and the tier 2 grading above was argued for the 1857 body — Hubbard's recollection through a named interviewer — not for the editorial apparatus around it. So `wolf_point_tavern.form.sign_mount` is graded `inferred` and not higher, and the device painted on the board is `reconstructed`; see docs/LIBERTIES.md L165. What would settle it is the passage's own origin — it has the shape of an Andreas paragraph or a Fergus reminiscence, and neither has been matched to it.
